blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this SIGCOMM'20 paper as a critical first measurement study assessing whether real-world 5G deployments live up to their hype. The study, conducted on a commercial 5G network (Non-Standalone Architecture) on a university campus, reveals significant gaps between promised and actual performance. Key findings include poor coverage with 8.07% coverage holes (vs. 3.84% for 4G), severe throughput degradation during handovers (80% drop), and inefficient TCP performance due to mismatched buffer sizes in wireline networks. While 5G achieves lower latency (21.8ms vs. 32% higher on 4G), it still falls short of the 10ms target for real-time applications like VR. The paper emphasizes that 5G's potential requires co-evolution of wireline paths, protocols, and hardware architectures, particularly for indoor coverage and energy efficiency.
paper_title: Understanding operational 5G: a first measurement study on its coverage, performance and energy consumption
paper_abstract: 1 5G, as a monumental shift in cellular communication technology, holds tremendous potential for spurring innovations across many vertical industries, with its promised multi-Gbps speed, sub-10 ms low latency, and massive connectivity. On the other hand, as 5G has been deployed for only a few months, it is unclear how well and whether 5G can eventually meet its prospects. In this paper, we demystify operational 5G networks through a first-of-its-kind crosslayer measurement study. Our measurement focuses on four major perspectives: (i) Physical layer signal quality, coverage and hand-off performance; (ii) End-to-end throughput and latency; (iii) Quality of experience of 5G’s niche applications (e.g., 4K/5.7K panoramic video telephony); (iv) Energy consumption on smartphones. The results reveal that the 5G link itself can approach Gbps throughput, but legacy TCP leads to surprisingly low capacity utilization (< 32%), latency remains too high to support tactile applications and power consumption escalates to 2 − 3× over 4G. Our analysis suggests that the wireline paths, upper-layer protocols, computing and radio hardware architecture need to co-evolve with 5G to form an ecosystem, in order to fully unleash its potential. We are standing on the eve of the 5G era. Major US cellular operators such as Verizon and AT&T already rolled out their first 5G deployment in 2019. Meanwhile, China’s three major mobile service providers officially launched commercial 5G services, and have deployed more than 150 thousand 5G base stations by the end of 2019 [77]. 13.7 million of 5G-enabled smartphones have been sold within less than a year [94]. It is widely reported that 5G represents a giant leap beyond 4G. It is expected to attain multi-Gbps wireless bit-rate for bandwidth-hungry applications like 4K/8K UHD video/VR transmission, ultra reliable and low latency communication (uRLLC) for auto-driving or telesurgery [92] and also the massive machine to machine communication for IoT [66...
